summaries.example: Imagine two toy boats that look alike from the outside. Their hidden parts might be arranged differently, so they could move differently in water. For Locke, the hidden arrangement that causes what a thing can do is like its real essence. The features we notice and use to name it—such as its shape and color—help form its nominal essence.
summaries.summary: John Locke separates two meanings of “essence,” or what makes something what it is. A real essence is the hidden inner constitution of a physical object. It causes the qualities we can observe, such as color, weight, or ability to bend. A nominal essence is an abstract idea that people make from qualities they notice together and then attach to a name. For example, our idea of gold may include being yellowish, heavy, and able to bend. Locke says people use nominal essences to sort things into named groups. We do not know the real essences of physical substances well enough to use them for ordinary classification. This helps explain why knowing the name of a substance is not the same as knowing its deepest nature. Locke also contrasts physical substances with mathematics and morality, where definitions can serve as both kinds of essence. Philosophers disagree about whether Locke thought nature itself contains natural kinds based on real essences, or whether he was mainly explaining how people make classifications.
key_ideas: A real essence is the hidden basis that makes a physical thing have its observable qualities.
A nominal essence is our general idea of the features shared by things that we place in one named group.
We can observe qualities, but Locke says we do not have a full idea of the hidden real essence of physical substances.
Because we do not know real essences, our names and classifications of physical things depend on the ideas we can form.
For shapes such as triangles, the definition can give us both the nominal and real essence; physical substances are different because their inner constitution is unknown.
summaries.why_it_matters: This distinction helps us notice the difference between how something appears, how we name it, and what causes its behavior. It also raises a lasting question: do our categories discover patterns already in nature, or do people partly create them? That question matters in science, language, and everyday thinking.

important_terms.definition: What makes a thing the kind of thing it is. For a physical object, Locke connects it with a hidden inner arrangement that causes the qualities we notice.
A general idea we make from qualities that similar things share, and then connect to a name such as “gold” or “penguin.”
A feature or power of a thing that can produce an idea in our minds, such as a color, sound, taste, or ability to melt wax.
A grouping or kind made by putting similar things under a shared name.

questions_to_think_about: Can two things look alike but work differently because their hidden parts differ?
Which features would you choose to define a group of objects?
Does a name tell us everything about what a thing really is?
Why might scientists need more than appearances to understand a substance?

summaries.example: Suppose two watches are both called watches because they show time and fit the ordinary idea linked to that name. One may use four wheels and another five; one may use a spring while another uses a different mechanism. Locke’s point is that a hidden difference in internal structure does not automatically create a new species. Whether the difference is “essential” depends on the complex idea associated with the name. Yet the internal structures may still explain why the watches behave as they do. This illustrates Locke’s division: nominal essence classifies, while real essence explains.
summaries.summary: Locke introduces “real essence” to distinguish the underlying basis of a thing from the idea by which we classify it. In material substances, the real essence is an internal constitution that produces observable qualities. A nominal essence, by contrast, is an abstract idea formed from qualities found together and used as the meaning of a general name. Thus, the nominal essence of gold might include a collection of visible, measurable, and reactive features, while its real essence would be the unknown structure responsible for them. Locke’s account divides two explanatory tasks that Scholastic substantial forms and some corpuscular theories assign to one entity: determining what species a thing belongs to, and explaining its qualities. He gives reasons to doubt that hidden structures determine species, including variation among members of one named group and the difficulty of deciding which internal differences count as species differences. Still, the entry emphasizes that Locke’s arguments are debated rather than obviously decisive. Scholars also disagree about whether real essence is relative to a nominal kind, whether individuals have real essences before classification, whether natural kinds exist for Locke, and how real essence relates to internal constitution and substratum. For simple ideas and modes, such as a triangle, Locke holds that real and nominal essence coincide, making mathematical and moral knowledge different from knowledge of substances.
key_ideas: Locke assigns two jobs that earlier theories often gave to one essence: nominal essences classify substances, while real essences causally explain their observable qualities.
Nominal essences arise through abstraction: we notice similarities, form a general idea, attach a name, and sort particular things under it.
A physical substance’s real essence is not available to us as a complete idea, so our knowledge of substances remains limited.
Locke’s distinction challenges the Scholastic idea that an immaterial substantial form both determines species membership and causes a thing’s properties.

The entry presents competing interpretations: real essence may mean the microstructure relevant to a nominal kind, or the substance’s total microstructure; it may belong only to sorted things or also to individuals.

Whether Locke allows natural kinds based on real essences is unresolved. His remarks can suggest that classifications track nature, but other passages emphasize variation within named groups and the role of human judgment.
summaries.why_it_matters: Locke’s distinction connects metaphysics, language, and science. It asks whether categories such as “gold” describe nature’s own divisions or organize observations according to human purposes. It also explains why a successful definition may let us reason with mathematics, while a definition of a substance does not by itself reveal the hidden causes of all its powers. The issue remains important whenever scientists classify things whose underlying structures are only partly known.

important_terms.definition: For a material substance, the underlying constitution that causes its observable qualities. Locke generally treats it as unknown to us, though interpreters debate its exact scope.
The abstract idea containing the features used to define and classify a species or genus under a name.

A power of a body to produce an idea in us. Primary qualities belong to the body; secondary qualities are powers to produce sensations such as color or sound; tertiary qualities are powers to change other bodies.
An internal physical makeup of a substance. Some interpreters treat this as equivalent to real essence, while others distinguish the terms.
A supposed underlying entity that supports the qualities of a thing. Locke’s discussion of substance or substratum concerns what it is to be a thing rather than merely a property.
A grouping that exists independently of human naming or classification. Scholars debate whether Locke accepts such groupings based on real essences.
The view associated with Scholastic natural philosophy that immaterial forms make matter belong to a species and cause its characteristic properties.

questions_to_think_about: If two objects share all the features in a definition but differ internally, are they the same kind?
Does ignorance of a real essence prevent us from making useful scientific classifications?
Can a classification be human-made without being random or arbitrary?
Should “internal constitution,” “real essence,” and “substratum” be treated as the same concept?
Why can a triangle have a known essence while a physical substance such as gold does not?

summaries.example: Your class might group mystery liquids by what you can observe: one is clear, another is cloudy, one smells strong, and one reacts with a test strip. That group rule is like a nominal essence: it uses shared qualities to give things a name or category. But two liquids that look the same might have different hidden particles and therefore react differently. Those hidden causes would be closer to real essences. The example also shows why a category can be useful without revealing everything about the things inside it.
summaries.summary: Locke’s idea of real essence concerns what makes a thing what it is beneath its observable features. For physical substances, he connects it with an inner constitution that causes qualities such as color, weight, texture, or the power to affect another body. A nominal essence is different: it is the general idea people create by collecting qualities that seem to occur together and using that idea to define a named group. We use nominal essences when we sort objects into species or genera, and we can do this without knowing their hidden structure. Locke uses this distinction against an older Scholastic picture in which an immaterial substantial form both made an object a member of a natural species and caused its properties. He argues that variation and borderline cases make that picture difficult, while his own account allows different inner structures among objects given the same name. However, the philosophical interpretation is not settled. Some passages suggest that our classifications may reflect real similarities in nature; others stress that deciding which differences matter depends on our ideas and names. The entry also examines whether individuals have real essences before classification and how real essence relates to internal constitution and substance. Locke says that for simple ideas, modes, mathematics, and morality, real and nominal essences coincide, whereas they come apart for physical substances.
key_ideas: Locke distinguishes the hidden cause of a substance’s qualities from the human idea used to classify it.
People form nominal essences by noticing similarities, choosing which qualities matter, and attaching names.
The same named group may contain objects with different hidden structures and different additional properties.
Locke’s view was partly a criticism of Scholastic substantial forms, which were said to do both the classifying and explaining jobs.
Scholars debate whether Locke believed there are natural kinds based on real essences, even though he clearly says our named species depend on abstract ideas.
In mathematics and morality, Locke treats the nominal and real essences of concepts as the same, unlike physical substances.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction helps separate three questions: what a thing is called, what features we use to recognize it, and what hidden structure causes its behavior. That separation is useful for understanding scientific limits and disagreements about classification. It also introduces a major philosophical problem: when we divide the world into kinds, are we discovering nature’s structure, shaping it with language, or doing some of both?

important_terms.definition: The underlying constitution of a physical thing that makes it have the qualities we can observe. Locke says we do not have a complete idea of it.
The abstract collection of qualities that people use to define a named group, such as a kind of metal or animal.
A power of an object to cause an idea or change. Color and sound are examples of effects produced in us; melting wax is an effect produced in another body.
A hidden physical arrangement or makeup that may explain a substance’s observable behavior.
A group believed to exist in nature independently of human naming. The entry treats Locke’s position on this as disputed.
An older theory’s immaterial form that was supposed to make a thing belong to a species and cause its properties.

questions_to_think_about: Can a useful category still leave out important hidden differences?
Who decides which similarities matter when a group is given a name?
Would knowing the particles inside a substance settle what kind it is?
Why might Locke think triangles are easier to know than pieces of metal?
Does “human-made” mean that a classification is completely arbitrary?
